source.title: Superposition unifies power-law training dynamics
source.authors: Z. Chen; Hao Chen; Yizhou Liu; Jeff Gore

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Uses a synthetic teacher-student model and MSE training dynamics rather than language-model pretraining loss, to examine power-law exponents and a compute-optimal width trend.
record.gate_note: The study tests training-time loss dynamics and a toy compute-versus-width frontier. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy in language models. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as results. The learned-embedding comparison changes the parameter count, so it is not a fixed-parameter-count test of V4.
record.test_reason: All empirical results come from a synthetic linear teacher-student model trained with MSE on sparse synthetic inputs. No language model is trained and no held-out pretraining loss is measured. The scaling-law versions name language-model loss and allocation (V1–V4, V6) or real modalities and regimes (V5). V7 concerns why published LM laws disagree. The paper frames its results as relevant to LLMs but does not test any version on that kind of system. Its findings are a different construct (toy-model training-time exponents and a toy width-compute frontier), so they go under fits_no_version rather than as tests. Labelling them V3 or V7 evidence would treat a toy-model analogy as a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim superposition gives up to a tenfold mid-training acceleration over sequential learning (e.g. α≈0.09 to ≈1 at a=1.1, b=0). They conclude that random embeddings are near-optimal for mid-training exponents. They say the origin of α≈1 remains open, alongside extensions to attention or multi-layer models and to late training.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a synthetic teacher-student model with sparse inputs, a diagonal teacher, random or learnable embedding matrices, and MSE loss; measures training-time dynamics and a toy compute-width frontier rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: The exponent depends on input and channel statistics without superposition; the reported superposition exponent is approximately invariant across tested input decay, channel decay and student sizes. The study compares fixed random with learnable embeddings and distinguishes mid-training from late-training plateau behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: In a toy teacher-student model without superposition, the training-loss exponent in time is α=(a+2b−1)/a, set by input and channel statistics. With a random superposition bottleneck, it becomes ≈1 across a, b and K, including with learnable embeddings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition makes power-law training-time loss exponents universal (≈1) and independent of data statistics.

fits_no_version.finding: In the toy model, optimal student width grows with compute as roughly K∝C^0.27 (preliminary fit), and iso-compute curves show minima.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Toy superposition models reproduce a compute-optimal width frontier.

fits_no_version.finding: The final plateau loss scales with toy width as K^−1.30±0.01.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capacity-limited loss in superposition toy models follows a width power law.

record.problems: The evidence uses a synthetic teacher-student model and MSE rather than language-model pretraining; the study fixes N=1024 and reports the main universal exponent only for its tested mid-training regimes. The compute-optimal frontier is a toy width-versus-compute experiment, with plotted iso-compute minima but no numerical minimum values stated. The authors identify extension to multi-layer architectures and more detailed late-training analysis as future work.
record.rows_left_out: No other distinct claim-relevant outcomes were omitted. Results on the theoretical clustered and isotropic limiting cases in Appendix A.2 are analytic mechanisms rather than additional empirical outcome rows; cited findings from prior studies were excluded.

untested.parts: No LM held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No LM parameter/token compute-optimal allocation. Only a toy width-versus-compute fit.
No other modality, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
No comparison of LM fitting choices, parameter counting or schedules.

missing.what: Learnable embeddings lower absolute loss by O(10^-3) against loss of O(10^-2), with the exponent unchanged.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with V3 and V7 labels was rejected. The system is a synthetic linear teacher-student MSE model, not a language model, and the versions name LM pretraining loss and allocation. LLM relevance is asserted by the authors, not measured. If curators accept toy models as a 'new setting', R6 could be reconsidered as T3 evidence on V3, but only for width-versus-compute. R6 is called a preliminary, rough fit, and no token-count allocation is tested.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy as a function of parameters, tokens or compute.
Does not fit loss laws on smaller runs and compare predictions with larger runs.

Tests only toy-model optimal student width against compute, using C=t×K². Does not test optimal token counts, equal parameter/token growth, or the Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann comparison in language-model pretraining.
Compares fixed and learnable embeddings, but does not hold parameter count fixed while varying depth, width or other architecture details.
Does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Does not measure downstream task performance.

Tests how toy-model training exponents vary with input and channel statistics, superposition, and fixed versus learnable embeddings. Does not test parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, fitting-method sensitivity, or disagreement between the original language-model scaling-law studies.

rows.subject: teacher-student model (no superposition)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the power-law exponent of the training loss without superposition; the paper also derives its predicted exponent.
rows.value: α=(a+2b−1)/a; empirical exponents are reported to match the prediction precisely.
rows.note: The paper says this exponent is governed by the input and channel statistics.
rows.check: Toy no-superposition training-loss exponent versus time, not LM scaling. This is the paper's own analytic baseline, so it should not be a V7 row.

rows.subject: teacher-student model (fixed random superposition embeddings)
rows.size_stated: N=1024; K∈[32,1024] in the experiment sweep
rows.operation_detail: Measured fitted power-law exponents of the mid-training loss under superposition.
rows.baseline: No-superposition case, whose exponent depends on a and b
rows.value: α≈1, reported as independent of a, b and compression ratio K/N.
rows.note: The paper describes the mid-training exponent as universal in the tested superposition regime.
rows.check: Toy mid-training exponent under fixed random embeddings. It does not measure LM loss or exponent disagreement across scaling-law setups.

rows.subject: teacher-student model (learnable W), K=128
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fitted mid-training loss exponent after making encoder and decoder embeddings learnable.
rows.baseline: Fixed-random embeddings are described as having the same α≈1 regime; a per-K baseline value is not stated.
rows.note: The paper calls this indistinguishable from the fixed-random-embedding α≈1 regime.
rows.check: Learnable-embedding toy exponent (1.0812±0.0215). Not an LM scaling measurement.

rows.subject: teacher-student model
rows.operation_detail: Extracted optimal student size from the compute-optimal frontier and fit its scaling with compute.

rows.check: Optimal width K versus compute C=t×K² in the toy model, which is not LM parameter/token allocation. The authors call the 0.2702 fit preliminary and a rough estimation; that caveat is missing from the row.
